college-cost-calculator.assumptionNote: Assumes constant education inflation, a constant savings return, and equal monthly contributions with no withdrawals.
benefits: Turns a scary future bill into one clear monthly number.
Shows the true cost of waiting to start saving.
Accounts for inflation instead of pretending today's fees will hold.
Gives you a concrete target to automate with a monthly investment.

faqs.a: Faster than general inflation. In India, quality private college fees have risen roughly 6–10% a year for a decade; in the US the long-run average is around 3–4% above general inflation. This calculator defaults to 6% — adjust it to match the colleges you are actually considering.
faqs.q: How fast do college costs really rise?

faqs.a: Because each year's fees inflate separately. Year two costs 6% more than year one, year three 6% more than year two, and so on. Over four years that compounding adds roughly 9% on top of four times the first-year figure.
faqs.q: Why is the 4-year total so much bigger than 4x the first year?

faqs.a: A lump sum invested today grows the most because every rupee compounds for the full period. But most families cannot spare one, so disciplined monthly saving is the realistic path — and starting today beats waiting for a lump sum that may never come.
faqs.q: Is it better to save monthly or invest a lump sum?

faqs.a: Be conservative. Equity-heavy portfolios have delivered 10–12% long-term in India, but with real volatility. Many planners use 8–10% for horizons over 10 years and lower the assumption as college approaches. Never assume the best historical return.
faqs.q: What return should I assume on savings?

faqs.a: Yes — add them to the annual cost input. For many students, accommodation, food, travel, and books add 30–50% on top of tuition. It is better to overestimate now than to fall short later.
faqs.q: Should I count hostel and living costs?

faqs.a: The monthly target jumps sharply because compounding has less time to help. Rerun the calculator with 5 years: you will see the monthly figure roughly triple. At that point, combining savings with a part-time education loan or targeting scholarships becomes realistic planning, not failure.
faqs.q: What if I start late, with only 5 years left?

college-cost-calculator.formula:
Future annual cost = present cost x (1 + inflation)^years.
4-year total = FV x ((1 + inflation)^4 - 1) / inflation.
Monthly saving PMT = total x i / ((1 + i)^N - 1), where i = monthly return, N = months until college.
howTo: Enter what one year of college costs today.
Set the expected yearly rise in education costs.
Enter how many years until college starts.
Set the return you expect on your savings, then read the monthly target.
keyFacts: Education inflation usually runs at 6–10% a year, well above general inflation.
A degree's total price is roughly four times the first-year cost, plus inflation each year.
Starting 15 years early can cut the required monthly saving to less than half of a 7-year plan.
Investment returns compound too — a 10% return does roughly a third of the work for you.
Fees are only part of it: hostel, travel, and living costs often add 30–50%.

college-cost-calculator.quickAnswer: If college costs ₹500,000 a year today and education inflation runs at 6%, one year will cost ₹1,198,279 in 15 years, and a 4-year degree will cost about ₹5,242,011 in total. Saving ₹12,647 every month at a 10% return gets you there. Starting early is the real trick — delay costs more than market timing ever could.
